posts.author: Dutchelm05
posts.content_md:
Boy three month sure goes by fast 

After some conversations with some of the good folks on the forum, I'm returning early.

One of the issues I see for many of the top DCG folks is the reoccurrence of the same questions regarding DCG. Whitening, film issues, too dark etc etc. If you look in the archives you can see similar problems. I like the idea Danny had which is a "Hero Kit", in it, is some essentials for making a good DCG from one of the gurus. In the event a beginner is experiencing problems, a kit can be sent, along with instructions and they can try it. Then, with all of known good ingredience, troubleshooting would become easier. If Danny wishes to be the care taker of such a hero kit, it would be welcomed.

Now to my question: What are the great unknowns still out there in DCG? What is the next level, if any, that DCG currently lacks? Are we there yet? Is it as bright as it could be? Consistency? Noise? What would constitute a perfect DCG hologram?

The reason that I ask is I believe squeezing out the last 10% of goodness is the hardest part in most endeavors. Even I get a little tired of shooting average to slight above average holos. BUT, when I talked to John the other day, he still gets excited over his holo of an elephant, it still takes his breath away. I have one in my office in which every time I pass by it I get transfixed. It is those seemly rare ones that crop up and has the certain something.

Perhaps it is the holos composition, or brightness or some intangible. Perhaps if we knew what it was we can devise test to understand it. We even have an artist willing to help us out 

Thanks for indulging me, you may be wondering why I didn't take the entire 3 months off by now

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
Good to see you back, Dutchelm05 

My interest in holography has been sustained for many years (now more than ever). The reason I'm so interested is because of its potential to become art. That's the whole key. You have to look at art first, then holography second. People continuously fail in holography, and lose interest, because they see holography first, and then try to "capture the real world in a three-dimensional nutshell," to borrow a really inane phrase from Hans Bjelkhagen. You can make a science demonstration, even with a hologram so good that it's difficult to tell it from reality. But so what? This may be interesting for a while, but it soon becomes isipid. Well, I certainly can't speak for everyone, but's that's my view.

An interest in holography can only be sustained if you have enough objectivity to throw Holography into the trash can, if that's where it belongs. This is what I mean by putting art first, and holography second. The problem is that people in general don't give a damn about art. They want gimmicks to make a few bucks, so they can buy consumer products (drugs).

But to answer your question Tony, I would say take up sculpture, but sculpture based on the parameters established by DCG. This is exciting and challenging, and I can't imagine losing interest.

posts.author: Dutchelm05
posts.content_md:
Thanks so much Joe,

You have touched on a very profane aspect of this subject and could not agree more. Art is the area of holographry I look forward to the most. My approuch thus far has been as many artist do, to copy others in there craft. Since DCG is the medium we use here we strive to perfect that craft by making brighter, cleaner images and control factors such as color, tone and contrast. Once that is achieved then art can be applied. The more technical control we have the broad the range of art we can under take.

So I guess Joe, if I can follow up, is there something in the DCG side that you feel can be improved, explored or better understood to better you ability to make art?

Thanks,

Tony

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
> **Dutchelm05:** Since DCG is the medium we use here we strive to perfect that craft by making brighter, cleaner images and control factors such as color, tone and contrast. Once that is achieved then art can be applied.

I disagree, Tony. Art needs to be present from very beginning, even before the first hologram is done. As I said, art comes first, and holography second. If it's about art, then it's about art, period. Holography might be the way to get there (the medium or the craft), but then again, it may not. If you try to perfect the technical side of holography exclusively, you will be wasting valuable time that is needed to work out the sculptural problems. Personally, I've been working on these sculptural problems exclusively for the last six months, and no "holography" per se. This takes considerable time, and a quick "burst of effort" will not work. So that's why I recommend taking up sculpture immediately, even at the expense of lab time for holography. To make good sculpture for DCG is not easy, and once your DCG problems are solved, you don't want to drop DCG for a year or two while you learn sculpture. Everyting needs to be pursued at once, as far as art is concerned, because you need to know how all the pieces will fit together.

One of the things over looked here , maybe because its much easyer to make a simple denisyuk hologram. Is lighting and beam ratio,and good undersanding of lighting. Light makes the diffrence of just taking a hologram of a object, to making the object stand out with dramtic light. It would be like those that just take a picture and those who take time and experence to make a masterpeace (art), To do this takes a multi beam setup and would be best to make a trans holo H1 first. 

 The reason most pro's use image plane refections to do ther DCG is because it gives better control over object placement and beam ratio's and one to one is best for a nice bright DCG. 

Also with this is to know how light works and how it refracts through the meduim (bends the light) 

This is why the angle of the reference beam used for recording is so important and a understanding of the formula so that the color of your center wave is optimised for maxuim replay of that color, most will change the forumla trying to get a color but not change the angle of there reference beam and wonder why they don’t get a good color control. You can understand this more by reading up on raindows or the ralcon papers [http://www.xmission.com/~ralcon/dcgprocess/p1.html](http://www.xmission.com/~ralcon/dcgprocess/p1.html)

I use two tests, one is to measure the light not reflected by the hologram. Before the back is painted place a light meter where the hologram will be displayed with the reconstruction light on. Then place the hologram infront of the hologram. The ratio is a rough guess as to the efficiency.

The rub is when the hologram has a reflection. Danny's Penguin is a great example (sorry for picking this as an example ). While much of the light was reflected, a large percentage of the light was being reflected in a gold tone specular reflection. It left a very nice gold square on the floor in front of the hologram. This reflection detracted from the light forming the image. Bob and I pondered the source of the reflection and speculated that it was a proximity copy with no index matching fluid. However if I remember right it was an H2 from a transmission master.

I would have to say for that top notch super bright DCG hologram, this is one of the most important aspects.

Tony, if you do a reflection test of your coins I doubt you are getting 100% reflection. Not to mention after the light goes through the plate a lot is absorbed. So even if the coins theorettically reflected 100%, you will not get to that optimal ratio. The coins is a very good starting point but I don't think they will be as bright as a reflection made from a transmission.

In my playing with some transmisison masters, it has come to my conclusion that they are the best way to get that super bright DCG. Being able to fine tune that ratio really helps. Reflection copies from reflection masters are "set" in the ref to obj ratio. While you can get some bright Reflections from reflections, you don't have the lattitude to adjust the object beam brightness.

As far as knowing if your are at the upper limit of DE, I would say if you adjusted the object beam in a H1 trans to H2 DCG reflection such that the object beam was brighter then the reference beam and you say the "glowing Halo" around the object they back off the object light until no halo is present, the fine tune the exposure and you should be at the maximum brightness that object can produce.

I think one of the Great unknowns in DCG, is learning to control the medium for max tonal control, I can see several way to do this, lighting, beam ratios, processing, exposer.

In photography the pros used transparencies, neg film, and paper. The negative was the one that had the most recorded tonal range, next was paper, and then slide film which had narrow tonal range like 3 stops.

In the trans hologram it a lot like the neg in that it can record a large range of tonal brightness, but just like in photography getting the tones to fit in a refection format takes some work, even more so in DCG.

DCG is alot like slide film in that it has a narrower tonal range. I remember a trick we used to do when shooting slide film when shooting flowers we would take 100 asa films and shoot it at 50 asa, then when we processed it in the first developer I would cut the processing time in half. Now what that did is squashed the tonal ranges and came out with nice gradual variations of tones and deep colors.

I know this can be done with the H1 and H2 silver or DCG.

I remember the holograms I saw over at bill Hilliard house, he had this one of a game board in plastic it was a DCG it was nice even tones with a vast tonal range. It was like I was holding the real board… wow

This has been a bit of my studies in applying the zone system to holography… I sorry if I got a bit heavy here , this has been one of the Great unknowns in DCG and sliver I have been trying to uncover

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md: With DCG it's really assumed that the hologram is going to be very bright. I would just buy some commercially-made DCG images, if you don't have them already, then you will have an idea about the typical brightness. I wouldn't get stuck on the brightness issue. Do you have some of A. Muth's holograms? If not, I would buy a few of the small ones, or a single bigger one. Then you will have a benchmark from a leader in DCG technique. I have one by him that's an image-plane holo, it's broadband and extremely bright. I use this for comparison. Another thing you can do is make a hologram of a mirror, which will show what a 1:1 ratio can accomplish (likely it will be dazzling bright). DCGs can really diffract a tremendous amount of light. I don't see any reason why a properly-made split beam master reflection hologram can't be just as bright as a H2. The only thing with the H2 is that you can cause the image to straddle the plane, or pop out in front, which, to be honest, I never thought too highly of. In my opinion, the very highest quality holograms are split beam master holograms, not H2's or copies. But by "highest quality" I'm taking all factors into consideration; cleanliness, brightness, noise, parallax, etc.

Hey Dave, Ima little confused. 

I have never known any holograhic recording material to have a DE of 100%, not even AmDi and coupled with the fact that 100% of the light will not pass through the H2 to be used for reconstruction of the H1, I am not sure how your are achieving a 1:1 ratio with a proximity reflection to reflection copy.

Example: At as close to brewsters as possible and negating the fact the light passing through the H2 bends it a little off brewster hitting the H1...if the polymer has a DE of 80% and the H2 absorbes 15% then only 68% of the reference beam is used as the object beam yielding a ratio close to 2:1. And 80% I thought was good for polymers and 15% absorbtion may be a little low depending on how much AmDi is in the emulsion.

My point is surely not to take away from your statement that your holograms are bright. And I can surely see the benifit of using a more efficient medium then silver but I have to argue that using a split beam such that you can adjust the object beam intensity is really the only way to get that close to 1:1.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Well, I believe there are two theories and I actually believe both theories are true depending on how you process your DCG.

The first is, a simple difference of index of refraction between the unexposed (less dense and a lower index of refraction) and the exposed (more dense and a higher index of refraction). It is this differential that refract or bends the light into the image. Here is it gel/gel.

The second is, during processing the unexposed regions are actually emptied of some gelatin and water and processed in such a way that an air void (or crack if you will) forms there. Again it is this differential that refracts or bends the light into the image. Here is it gel/air.

This really should be studied to see which method works best for the outcome one is trying to produce (broadband, narrow band, reflection, transmission).

I would have to say for transmission it would cause the replay angle to change more for the latter then the former due to a greater bending. But probably not enough to effect display work.

See here

[http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/hframe.html](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/hframe.html)

I would have to say in a reflection it would cause a higher percentage of light per fringe to be reflected thus increasing efficiency of the individual fringes.

See here

[http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/hframe.html](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/hframe.html)

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
R. K. Curran and T. A. Shankoff 

Applied Optics, Vol. 9, Issue 7, pp. 1651-1657 

Abstract

Experiments have been performed which lead to the conclusion that dichromated gelatin holograms arise as a result of the formation of an air-gelatin interface, with the observed high diffraction efficiencies resulting from the air-gelatin refractive index differential of 0.52 found at the interface. It is postulated that rapid removal of water by isopropanol in the development process creates strains in the gelatin film which are relieved by splitting. The resultant cracks in the hologram manifest themselves in an obvious location, between the highly exposed planes of cross-linked gelatin. Photomicrographic evidence on Bragg-Lippmann and on plane gratings, liquid gate data, lack of thickness reciprocity for the gratings, and observations of grating thickness employing bandpass measurements comprise the bulk of the experimental work. From these data, a model is proposed that is consistent with all the experimental results for both Bragg-Lippmann and plane gratings.
